newsitem.title: USA: Oregon property tax measure may be rewritten - paper.
newsitem.headline: Oregon property tax measure may be rewritten - paper.

text.p: Measure 47, a controversial Oregon property tax limitation initiative, may be rewritten and submitted later this year to state voters, according to a published report on Wednesday.

"The idea basically is to write a new constitutional framework for the property tax and put it on the May or June ballot," said state Rep. Tom Brian, the House Revenue Committee chairman, according to the Oregonian.
The newspaper reported that Brian's plan would retain the property tax limits approved by voters in Measure 47 and would guarantee taxpayer savings.

Last November, voters in the state approved Measure 47, which stated that the amount of 1997-1998 property taxes must be based on property taxes from either tax year 1994-1995 or 10 percent less than 1995-1996, whichever value is less.
The idea to rewrite Measure 47 has gained momentum in the state Capitol because of a legal opinion released earlier this week by the state's attorney general, the Oregonian reported.
Because of the way Measure 47 was worded, many state lawmakers had assumed that taxes to repay bonds would not be included in the calculation of the state's tax base.
But according to the opinion issued by the state attorney general's office, taxes levied to pay off bonds should be included in the calculation.
If these bond taxes are included, the amount in the tax base would increase, which in turn would allow lawmakers to decrease the amount of tax relief provided under Measure 47.

If lawmakers follow the attorney general's opinion and include bond taxes in their property tax calculations, the amount of tax relief under Measure 47 could be reduced by as much as $500 million over the next two years, according to Deputy Oregon Attorney General David Schuman.
Brian, a Republican, was not immediately available to comment on the Oregonian report.
